articles.title_orig: How Ivanka Trump’s Guo Pei dress put Chinese high fashion in spotlight
articles.title_zh: How Ivanka Trump’s Guo Pei dress put Chinese high fashion in spotlight
articles.content_orig:
Viral video of broken brackets in test of car from Huawei-backed brand prompts ministry action to step up policing of quality
A safety failure spotted in tests of a Chinese electric vehicle (EV) made by a Huawei Technologies-backed luxury brand has raised doubts about the cars many consumers view as a source of national pride, and prompted regulators to step up policing of quality and reliability.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, along with three other ministry-level departments, published draft rules on Saturday that would govern testing of new car models. The move came after a video released on Thursday on ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi showed that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 EVs used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h.
“A car’s brake pedal should absolutely never fail while driving,” Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said in a commentary on Sunday.

articles.title_orig: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
articles.title_zh: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to exercise caution when flying in or around Saudi Arabia after deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, which have shut down the airport in the Saudi capital.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remains closed as of Monday after attacks that started last week. The attacks escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.
Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week.
The U.S., Australia and other countries advised citizens against travel to the region.
The FAA late Sunday said that pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. It said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." The FAA's warning is in effect until Dec. 10.
Most U.S. airlines don't fly to Saudi Arabia.
Delta Air Lines is scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23. CEO Ed Bastian said in an interview Thursday, before the Saturday missile attack, that "safety is going to make the call" on whether to operate the flight as planned. As of Sunday night, Delta hadn't changed its plans, a spokeswoman said.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says Ukraine supports 'energy ceasefire' announced by Trump - follow live
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says Ukraine supports 'energy ceasefire' announced by Trump - follow live
articles.content_orig:
A rescue worker puts out a fire at residential houses destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Andrii Marienko/AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"
Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.
"Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening."
The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia."
Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter."
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin "had one answer to all of them — 'nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world."
He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
"We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ."
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
"Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.
"With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy's term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
"Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.
Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.
"I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."
Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.
Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience." He said they affected "healthcare, and everything else."
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facility, Yandex said.
Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.
Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, according to Ivan Fedorov, former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council.
Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, with eight still hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

In May, the Pentagon sought congressional authorisation and funding to buy more than 12,000 Blackbeard missiles for deployment across the armed services over five years. US Navy projections put the average gross unit cost at about US$385,000 in the financial years 2028-31.
In contrast, the cost of Lockheed Martin’s larger Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) is estimated in US Air Force budget figures for the 2024 financial year to be about US$3.25 million.

articles.title_orig: Kelly Clarkson says a Brooklyn store snubbed her. The shop says the item she wanted wasn’t for sale.
articles.title_zh: Kelly Clarkson says a Brooklyn store snubbed her. The shop says the item she wanted wasn’t for sale.
articles.content_orig:
Kelly Clarkson accused a New York City store of treating her as though she couldn’t afford its merchandise. But the business at the center of her viral complaint offered a different explanation.
Clarkson, a three-time Grammy winner, publicly called out Art of Play in Brooklyn, writing Saturday on X that she visited the curiosity shop with “a few things in mind to buy” and was offered something similar after being treated as though she couldn’t afford what she wanted.
“Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote of the employee who served her at the store. She compared the experience to the scene in “Pretty Woman” in which Julia Roberts’ character is snubbed at an upscale boutique, urging people to visit the store “if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character.”
Clarkson’s accusation sparked swift backlash against Art of Play, leading many social media users to criticize it and leave negative online reviews.
Art of Play said Sunday in a statement on Instagram that Clarkson asked about purchasing Molly, a “one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton.” The mechanical bird wasn’t for sale, the store said, because it “plays an important role in the magic shows we host here.”
“However, the negative experience Kelly described on twitter would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged in a shop,” the store wrote. It added that all visitors to Art of Play are “equally welcome.”
The statement, which offered an explanation for why Clarkson couldn’t buy the bird, didn’t directly address her allegation that an employee had treated her as though she “couldn’t afford” its merchandise.
Art of Play described the reaction to Clarkson’s post as overwhelming.
“Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store,” it added. “It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity.”
Art of Play’s response Sunday fueled further debate online over whether Clarkson misinterpreted the interaction and whether her decision to publicly name the small business was warranted.
Representatives for Clarkson and Art of Play didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
In a post Sunday evening on X , Clarkson doubled down, accusing Art of Play of lying in its statement about the bird art being for sale.
“so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can,’” she wrote.
Clarkson said the store was “really cool” and she supports small businesses, “but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business.”
Early Monday morning, the Art of Play posted an additional statement responding to Clarkson’s last post. The store said that during her 5-minute visit, after she asked about the mechanical bird, they explained to Clarkson that while Molly “serves as a de facto mascot for our shop, a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines” and that he would be willing to part with the puppet for $15,000.
“We explained all of this to Kelly Clarkson. We also offered to show her a different singing bird automaton, made by a traditional clockmaking shop in Germany, that she could have taken home with her that day,” the store explained in an Instagram post. “It costs about $2,000. She did not stick around long enough to see it. We’ve reached out to Kelly directly to try and clear the air. We really do wish her the best and hope that someday we can all laugh about this misunderstanding.”
Clarkson is a coach on NBC’s “The Voice” and the former host of “The Kelly Clarkson Show,” which also aired on the network. NBC is a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.
The incident has ignited some discourse about whether bias plays into stores’ treatment of customers.
Some online speculated that Clarkson may have taken offense because she wasn’t recognized, while others argued that she was asking to be treated decently as a customer regardless of whether the business knew of her wealth and status.
In its statement, Art of Play thanked its community for its support and welcomed “all the curious folks who have discovered us amidst the drama.” The store also referred to one of Clarkson’s most famous lyrics.
“We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday,” Art of Play wrote. “As a talented popular singer once said ‘what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.’”
Angela Yang is a culture and trends reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.content_orig:
The all-stock deal includes up to $150 million in earnouts tied to Elisity's future performance
IonQ agreed to acquire Elisity, a cybersecurity firm, through an all-stock transaction worth as much as $1.3 billion, according to the Wall Street Journal. The companies planned to announce the transaction later Monday.
Of that total, as much as $150 million is structured as earnouts that depend on how Elisity performs going forward, according to the Wall Street Journal. The exchange ratio for IonQ shares in the deal is pegged to a reference price ranging from $33.07 to $49.61 apiece. IonQ stock closed Friday at $39.89, giving the company a market value of roughly $16 billion.
IonQ Chairman and Chief Executive Niccolo de Masi said the acquisition reflects his view that cybersecurity risks will grow as quantum computing and artificial intelligence systems become more capable. "The bad guys are going to keep taking advantage of new technology," de Masi told the Wall Street Journal. "Unfortunately, we are entering the most dangerous years, vis-à-vis cybersecurity risks."
De Masi said the combined company will aim to help customers guard against threats that involve AI agents. He also cited the looming risk of "Q-Day" — the point at which quantum computers could become powerful enough to break widely used public-key cryptography — as a reason American corporations and the U.S. government need to prepare, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Elisity, which launched in 2019, has built its business around software that blocks intruders and ransomware from propagating laterally through a network. Its customers include healthcare companies and hospitals. Elisity Chief Executive James Winebrenner is expected to stay on after the deal closes.
IonQ's core technology is the trapped-ion approach to quantum hardware, and the company counts clients in fields ranging from pharmaceutical research to defense. The company works with the U.S. Defense Department and has pursued a series of acquisitions to expand its capabilities. That buying spree included a $1.8 billion agreement earlier this year to take over semiconductor manufacturer SkyWater Technology, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The quantum-computing sector has drawn attention from Washington. Over the summer, President Donald Trump issued executive orders calling for accelerated development of a high-capability quantum computer and for shoring up federal defenses against the cyber risks such technology could enable, according to the Wall Street Journal.

articles.title_orig: MAGA Inc. plots final midterm money moves
articles.title_zh: MAGA Inc. plots final midterm money moves
articles.content_orig:
Political action committees supporting Republican Senate candidates have reported hundreds of millions of dollars in outside spending as the 2026 midterm elections approach, with major funds targeting key races across the country while President Donald Trump’s political operation has kept a large reserve of cash.
According to Legis1, the Senate Leadership Fund reported $173,991,698.46 in spending, directing opposition efforts across nine Senate contests. Ohio received $41.98 million, followed by North Carolina with $30.23 million and Michigan with $27.4 million.
The Senate Leadership Fund described its role in protecting the Republican Senate majority by saying, "it is the first line of defense to protect or Republican Senate majority." said SLF PAC, the Senate-focused political action committee.
Legis1 reported that Texas PAC ranked second with $133.56 million in cumulative outside spending, all focused on the Texas U.S. Senate contest. The group reported $68.82 million in support spending and $64.74 million in opposition spending.
The Texas Senate race has attracted $139.18 million in combined reported outside spending from the three largest PACs mentioned by Legis1. The general election is scheduled for Nov. 3, 2026, and the contest is rated a toss-up.
No Going Back PAC Inc., aligned with Trump’s movement, ranked third with $128,265,960.25 in reported spending. Its largest opposition expenditures targeted Ohio at $17.58 million, Michigan at $16.56 million and North Carolina at $8.73 million, according to Legis1.
MS NOW reported that Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC accumulated more than $400 million over the summer but has spent cautiously ahead of the midterms. The group reportedly began booking about $140 million in advertising through affiliated super PACs in mid-September after Republican officials sought more support.
A Trump aide explained the strategy by telling Time, "He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now," said a Trump aide.
The aide’s comments came amid discussion of whether Trump was prioritizing future political influence over immediate midterm spending. The same aide added, "He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities." said a Trump aide.
MS NOW reported that maintaining congressional control would affect Trump’s ability to advance legislation, appoint judges and respond to potential investigations. The report also noted that Trump’s fundraising capacity while in office could influence how he manages political resources after leaving office.

articles.title_orig: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
articles.title_zh: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
articles.content_orig:
US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies
Business live – latest updates
Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.
Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation” , giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).
“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.
These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time.
Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions.
Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP).
Woodfood built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now.
This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said.
Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows.
after newsletter promotion
Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”.
And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass.
Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news.
Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into fresh water and salt water varieties.
The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism.
Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies.

articles.title_orig: Skies over Saudi capital Riyadh largely empty after deadly Houthi strikes on airport
articles.title_zh: Skies over Saudi capital Riyadh largely empty after deadly Houthi strikes on airport
articles.content_orig:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.
Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in missile attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport over the weekend that killed at least 13 people.
Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.
The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.
After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.
“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”
So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.
Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.
Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.
“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”
Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.
The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.
AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.
Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.
Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.
Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.
How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”
Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.
Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.
“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”

articles.title_orig: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.title_zh: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.content_orig:
Light Reading, the globally recognized authority in communications industry media, has announced the winners of its 22nd Leading Lights Awards. The " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " jointly submitted by Huawei, China Unicom, and Peking University, stood out among 151 shortlisted projects worldwide, winning the Outstanding Use Case: Network Security & Resilience Use Case Award. This recognition marks a new chapter in the application of 5G private networks within the higher education sector. As AI-driven research and digital campus life accelerate across universities, faculty and students are placing greater demands on campus networks. Previously, access to internal campus resources relied on the traditional internet + VPN model. This approach carries security risks, including data leakage and account compromises. It also delivers a poor user experience, with high latency, unstable connections, and repeated login prompts. These shortcomings no longer meet the needs of modern universities. At the same time, conventional 5G private networks suffer from lengthy service provisioning cycles and elevated management costs. They are ill-suited to the high personnel turnover typical of academic institutions. Breaking through the security and experience bottlenecks of traditional VPN models  and enabling faculty and students to access campus resources securely and conveniently from anywhere outside campus  has become a shared priority in university IT modernization. In response, Huawei and China Unicom have jointly introduced the " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " solution  directly addressing the security risks and experience gaps faced by faculty and students accessing campus intranet resources from off-campus locations. The solution delivers a seamless upgrade in campus resource access: no VPN cluster, no annual licence planning, no SIM approval workflow. Zero-Touch Onboarding: Built on CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure), the federated authentication system of CERNET (China Education and Research Network), faculty and students can activate the 5G Mobile Private Network using their existing university credentials. A single phone  without changing SIM cards or phone numbers  provides seamless access to the campus network, eliminating the need to install or repeatedly start and stop VPN clients.
Light Reading judges commented: This architecture  The university, not the operator, remains the sole identity authority  carries significant replication potential. The solution leverages the existing CERNET infrastructure without requiring large-scale campus network modernization, and can be rapidly deployed across the universities already connected to CARSI. The 5G Free-Mobility Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, covering the core scenario of off-campus access to campus intranet resources. Faculty and students enjoy seamless campus network access with a single phone  no SIM change, no number change. During a three-month pilot involving over 100 faculty and students, more than 70% of respondents rated the new service as superior to traditional VPNs in stability, latency, and ease of use. Service provisioning time was reduced from several days to seconds, and the private network deployment cycle was compressed from approximately three months to three weeks. This solution provides a replicable model for 5G private network deployment across the universities connected to CARSI, with the potential for international extension. Looking ahead, Huawei will continue to deepen joint innovation with China Unicom across more universities  focusing on 5G-Advanced, 6G, network security, and AI-native networks (AIDN)  to advance the network-as-a-service vision in the education sector. By helping quality educational resources transcend campus boundaries, Huawei is committed to contributing a China-based solution and Chinas wisdom to global university digital transformation. FAQs: Q1: What is CARSI? CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure) is a unified identity authentication platform built by CERNET (China Education and Research Network). It now covers over 1,000 universities across China, enabling cross-institutional identity mutual recognition and resource sharing. Q2: What problem does the 5G Mobile Private Network solve? Traditionally, faculty and students must install VPN clients to access campus intranet resources  a process that introduces security risks and delivers a frustrating experience. With the 5G Free-Mobility Private Network, users reach the campus network seamlessly through China Unicoms 5G service. No new SIM card, no number change, no additional setup is needed. The system also resolves the management overhead caused by frequent faculty turnover and the continuous cycle of student enrollment and graduation, automatically terminating access when users leave the university. Q3: What application scenarios does the 5G Mobile Private Network currently support? The 5G Mobile Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, enabling faculty and students to access campus intranet resources using 5G data from off-campus locations. In the future, this solution can be rapidly replicated across the more than 1,000 universities connected to CARSI, and can extend to overseas universities through eduGAIN.

articles.title_orig: UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.title_zh: UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.content_orig:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Sunday became the first British leader to openly complain of Russian tampering in the Brexit referendum a decade ago.
Burnham, who took on the role in July from Keir Starmer, thinks leaving the European Union did "more harm than good" and has opened the door to closer ties, including possibly rejoining the bloc.
Burnham told The Rest Is Politics podcast that he had posed the question upon first arriving in Downing Street, and was given a "clear answer that yes, there was [a link to Russian interference]."
He did not provide evidence of the Kremlin's efforts to influence the June 2016 vote, where the UK decided to leave the EU by a 52% to 48% majority .
With the rise of far-right parties in the UK and across the EU, Burnham ​said voters needed better information about efforts by rogue states to disrupt their democracies.
"These things are important now to put clearly on the ​record, and I believe, ‌help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said.
Burnham described how German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had told him during talks in Berlin this week that the AfD is "clearly linked to Russia — funded, I believe.”
"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” Burnham added.
Burnham's Brexit remarks contrast with former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU. In 2020, Johnson said ​there was no evidence of Russian sway.
The UK Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government had failed to fully assess how Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts could have impacted the vote.
In its report, the Committee also found the Kremlin sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, which was rejected by voters.
The UK's intelligence agencies believe Russia continues to spread disinformation to undermine public trust, alongside cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage . They say the issue is getting worse and is often aided by artificial intelligence (AI).
Russia has long denied meddling in other countries' elections or referendums.
After the Brexit vote, it cast some British politicians as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. Last month, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.
Last month, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
EU officials have welcomed the change in tone from London, while France and Spain have spoken positively about closer ties, including rejoining.
Some experts remain skeptical, however. Professor Iain Begg of the London School of Economics thinks rejoining would reopen deep political divisions, be complicated from both the EU and UK sides and likely take years.

articles.title_orig: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.title_zh: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.content_orig:
What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.
The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology , came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.
Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.
How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging
At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.
Scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an important player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.
Earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.
The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.
They discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.
To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.
The results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.
Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.
Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days
The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?
To find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.
Just 30 days after treatment, the animals showed measurable improvements.
Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.
In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.
These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.
But the researchers also uncovered an important clue about how Menin produced these effects.
A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue
When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.
Amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other important functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.
D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.
Further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.
Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.
This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.
To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.
The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.
However, there was an important distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.
That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.
Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging
Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.
In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism , researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.
That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.
Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.
An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature .
The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells showed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.

articles.title_orig: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
articles.title_zh: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
articles.content_orig:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.
Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in missile attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport over the weekend that killed at least 13 people.
Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.
The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.
After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.
“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”
So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.
Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.
Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.
“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”
Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.
The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.
AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.
Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.
Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.
Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.
How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”
Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.
Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.
“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”
Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

articles.title_orig: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.title_zh: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.content_orig:
Rev. Serge Fornerod brings forty years of international experience in development, public administration and ecumenical relations. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall, he managed aid and development programmes in Eastern Europe and later contributed to international relations within the umbrella organisation for Switzerland’s Protestant Churches. Since retiring in 2023, he has remained active in ecumenical networks, supporting the Foundation for Aid to Reformed Protestantism and the John Knox International Reformed Centre in Geneva.
Rev. Fornerod is a former member of the World Council of Churches central committee. He is also involved in preparations for the 2027 Francophone Christian Forum and researches the spread of early Christianity, particularly in the East . He took time to reflect on a new blog he has created that documents his experience at the Near East School of Theology (NEST) in Beirut, and his thoughts on the key to Christian unity.
What inspired you to start your blog to document your experience at the Near East school of Theology in Beirut?
Rev. Fornerod: Through this blog, I ’ d like to share some reflections and convictions I have formed over the last few years within the ecumenical movement and in my personal life.
The first is that when a parent is unwell, seriously afflicted by illness for years on end, telling them – as I often read on social media from “ good Christians” and – sorry to say – even church leaders – “ we ’ re thinking of you” or “ our prayers are with you” only helps the person saying it. Potentially, such phrases eventually add to the parent ’ s suffering, leaving them feeling even more alone. Someone who is ill, someone in despair, someone rendered invisible and voiceless by misfortune and injustice – that is someone you visit. You must take the time to listen and truly understand what the other person is going through. I believe that the Christian West (in general) takes its responsibility towards situations of suffering in the world and the churches experiencing them far too lightly. If we truly believe that the faith and life of churches elsewhere in the world concern us directly, then we must talk less about “ solidarity” – when this has no impact on our daily lives – and take more action. "Witness is with-ness.”
The second message is that in the world of ecumenical relations or relations between churches, the key to unity is not primarily dialogue, but listening. In light of everything that has been happening in the Middle East for decades, but especially since October 2023, I wanted to come and listen to the voices of Christians on the ground. Back home in Switzerland – though I fear this may also be the case elsewhere – I had the impression that opinions were quickly set in stone regarding who the culprits and who the victims were. My limited experience of the Middle East so far has very quickly made me feel uncomfortable in the face of so many so-called certainties, which in fact conceal unacknowledged political and cultural preconceptions. I wanted to give more space to the concrete reality of people ’ s lives and the experiences of the churches here. To listen, one must step back from one ’ s own context; one must be prepared to remain silent for a long while; one must be prepared to place trust first and foremost in the person who is in that situation; and one must draw closer, physically as well. The NEST faculty, with its international and ecumenical identity—driven by young people and researchers rather than officials (whom I also meet frequently and with pleasure!)—strikes me as an ideal place for observation, networking, and gathering information.
What do you hope others gain from you sharing your learning pilgrimage?
Rev. Fornerod: I hope to raise awareness amongst as many readers as possible of the need to take the time to reflect and find out more before forming an opinion on what is happening in this region. But also to show that it is relatively easy to obtain insightful background information on people ’ s experiences and the living conditions under which people here must face these new challenges. Action is easily possible and effective. When you consult the local sources here, it is striking to see, for instance, how many people in Israel oppose the destruction campaign of the Israeli army and how many people in Lebanon are engaged in bringing help. And lastly to hear that, for the Christians here, there is quite simply no alternative but to hold their heads high and carry on fighting day in, day out for dignity and justice – whether in their personal lives, their country ’ s politics or international justice. And if there is a Westerner present at the gatherings where people pray for this here, then perhaps that might do a little good.
Can you describe the way in which you are engaging with people?
Rev. Fornerod: One of the very nice and positive aspects of “ just being here,” free enough to engage with people is indeed to see the ease, spontaneity, hospitality, and kindness with which the Lebanese respond to your presence, however surprised they might be. It is a life lesson to see that, in an international, national, economic, and social situation as complicated and desperate as the one here, people naturally manage to draw strength from and take pleasure in making you happy.

articles.title_orig: Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans
articles.title_zh: Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans
articles.content_orig:
​Elon Musk’s political operation is focused on the most consequential races of the midterm elections , according to a WIRED analysis of federal campaign finance data.
As of October 6, America PAC, the main Musk-affiliated super PAC, had deployed $24.8 million of the $31 million it has spent on this year’s races into seven key US Senate contests that are widely seen as close—if not toss-ups—and represent a path for Democrats to take control of the chamber this November.
To monitor America PAC’s spending in the midterms, WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where America PAC is putting money into the midterms, from individual races to Musk’s overall influence on the election season. It draws on America PAC’s filings with the Federal Election Commission (FEC), which the agency processes daily and which lists all the payments America PAC has made for ads, mailers, and texts.
America PAC appears, based on filings to date, smaller, and aimed differently, than it was two years ago. The $31 million it has spent on candidates so far this year is about a third of the $85.9 million it had spent on them by the same point in 2024, when more than 90 percent of that money went to the presidential race and almost none to Senate races. America PAC registered with the FEC in May 2024 and overall spent $261 million that cycle, with about 95 percent of its funding coming from Musk.
For this election cycle, most of America PAC’s spending has been concentrated on financing campaign efforts attacking Democrats, WIRED’s review shows. For every dollar spent supporting a Republican candidate, more than two went to opposing a Democrat, as of October 6. In Senate races, it was three.
The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this November because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds. The implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching for Musk in particular, who could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.
In the most fraught Senate races, where the GOP has been on the back foot, the ratio of negative to positive campaign messaging has been even more skewed, the filings show.
For the Senate race in Texas, where Musk lives and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based, the group has spent more than $9.4 million on ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and $1.8 million backing Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. In part due to a litany of past scandals, including a federal investigation into alleged misuse of office, which the Department of Justice closed without any charges brought against him, Paxton has trailed Talarico in every public poll since the middle of August. The most recent poll of registered voters by Marist University places Talarico 6 points ahead .
The largest single expenditures by America PAC in Texas have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. Most of the rest of the money has gone to paying for printed materials, postage, and campaign calls. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other outside groups.
In Iowa, the PAC has spent 14 times more money attacking Democrat Josh Turek than it has backing Republican Ashley Hinson. More than three-quarters of all Senate spending so far has gone to defending seats Republicans already hold.
Even in races where the disparity has been lower—for instance, in the Ohio Senate race—America PAC has spent double the amount attacking former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown as defending the record of incumbent Jon Husted.
Husted has faced a particularly bruising campaign, dogged by his support for the Iran war and battered by negative ads portraying him as “the face of data centers” because of a planned Nvidia data center project in the state that will be leased by OpenAI.
More generally, WIRED’s review of the filings submitted to the FEC shows that America PAC has spent more than $83 million boosting Republican candidates and causes since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.
More than half of that figure came in the first six months of 2025, including nearly $13 million on the Wisconsin Supreme Court race that the GOP lost—Musk had claimed the future of “Western civilization” was on the line—and $27 million on petition incentives. Prior to the election, America PAC posted on social media that it would pay people $100 to sign the petition and $100 per referral for that race. (Voting officials in the state alleged probable cause to believe that Musk’s offers of $1 million payments had violated election bribery laws, but prosecutors ultimately declined to bring charges .)
In between Musk’s public fallout with Trump last year and his return to politics this summer, the outflows from America PAC largely went quiet. Musk’s own checkbook did not. Between June 2025 and May 2026, he personally gave $40 million to other Republican groups.
And since late August, America PAC has whirred back into gear, throwing $11.2 million into the Texas Senate race and about $5 million each into the Ohio and Michigan Senate races, as well as $10.2 million in other House and Senate contests.
It isn’t clear yet how much America PAC has put into field operations and other get-out-the-vote efforts this year, though future filings will shed light on this. Nor is it clear who is paying for the surge. The group reported $274,171 in the bank at the end of June and has spent $31 million since; the donors behind the difference will not be disclosed until its next report, October 15. Through June, virtually all of its money had come from Musk. A spokesperson for the super PAC declined to comment.

articles.title_orig: Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status
articles.title_zh: Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status
articles.content_orig:
Measles is the most contagious disease known. It can rip through a population without immunity like wildfire. Just look at what's happening in Pennsylvania, says Patsy Stinchfield , executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a public health effort led by the National Infectious Diseases Foundation.
"In January in Pennsylvania, they had 12 cases. Now we're seeing 100 plus cases per week and over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania," she says. "If Pennsylvania can see it spread that fast, that can happen in any state that has low immunization rates."
As vaccination rates have fallen across the country, many communities have become vulnerable. Nationwide, more than 4,000 measles cases have been reported this year alone — the highest number in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported five deaths. New York state declared a measles emergency.
Stinchfield says the recent measles surge has got many people wondering if they're at risk.
"It's a very common question for people to ask, 'am I immune? Am I OK? What do I need to do?' And that is exactly the right question everyone should be asking themselves right now," Stinchfield says.
The best defense is vaccination. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective — meaning 97% of people will have an immune response.
"The measles vaccine is safe. It's highly effective, and it confers lifelong immunity," says Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of Booster Shots , a history of measles.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
But what if you don't know your immunization history, or you only got one dose of the measles shot? Should you get another dose? Infectious disease experts say that depends on several factors.
People born before 1957 are presumed to be immune because back then, measles was so common, just about everyone got it in childhood, says Dr. Larry Kociolek , a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
"It was thought that pretty much everyone in the U.S. was infected with measles as sort of a rite of passage in childhood," Kocielek says. He says anyone who's ever had measles can be confident they're protected.
That is of course, if you survived. Before vaccines, measles used to kill 400 to 500 people each year in the U.S.
People who were born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 may need an additional dose. That's because a small group of people who were immunized during that time received an early, less effective version of the vaccine that used inactivated or killed virus.
If you're not sure which vaccine you got, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends talking to your doctor about getting one or two doses of the MMR vaccine.
At first, children in the U.S. received just one dose of the MMR vaccine. But that changed in 1989, after public health officials determined that a single dose wasn't enough to prevent outbreaks. That year, the official recommendation switched to two doses of MMR vaccine for children, which is still in effect today.
Kids need the higher protection "because they tend to be at higher risk of exposure, since they're oftentimes in group settings like schools and daycares," Kociolek says.
One dose of MMR vaccine is 93% effective, and traditionally, Kociolek says, that was considered enough protection for most adults, unless they were at higher risk of being exposed to measles. Health care workers, people in a college setting and those travelling abroad are all in this group. If you live with or are in close contact with someone who is immunocompromised, you also need two doses of vaccine to protect them.
But given the recent, dramatic rise of measles across the country these days, "if you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose," Kociolek says.
Ratner says it's definitely worth asking your doctor if you should get a second dose.
While measles is often considered to be a childhood disease, a large proportion of people sickened this year have been unvaccinated adults — and people over 20 who lack immunity are at higher risk of serious complications.
No matter your age, "measles is a serious disease," Stinchfield says.
She notes that getting two doses of the vaccine can also help others at higher risk who can't get the MMR shot, including people who are pregnant, severely immunocompromised and infants under 6 months of age.
If you're just not sure if you're protected against measles and you can't find records of immunization, you could get a test to check your blood antibody levels. But those tests aren't perfect, says Dr. William Moss , a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
"It's possible that a person could actually be protected and test negative on one of those," Moss says.
Depending on your circumstances, your insurance might not cover the blood test. But most private insurance plans and Medicaid must cover another MMR vaccine at no cost.
Moss says if you can't confirm how many doses of MMR vaccine you've had, "I would say it is easier and less expensive to just get another MMR vaccine, and there is no harm in getting a second MMR vaccine or even a third, additional MMR dose."
After all, it's much better to be protected than infected.

articles.title_orig: The world's hottest AI stock market has gone cold
articles.title_zh: The world's hottest AI stock market has gone cold
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
South Korea went from the world's hottest stock market to its coldest in months.
Taiwan is pulling ahead as investors broaden AI bets beyond memory chips.
Asia's AI trade is expanding from memory chips to the broader hardware supply chain.
South Korea's stock market has gone from the world's hottest to its coldest in just a few months.
The Kospi, the world's best-performing major stock benchmark in the first half of 2026, has since fallen about 24%, making it the worst-performing major market in the second half. It's still more than 50% higher this year.
The AI trade isn't losing its appeal. But investors are increasingly looking beyond South Korea's memory-chip giants to companies with broader exposure to the AI hardware boom.
In July, analysts at GlobalData.TS Lombard pointed out that much of the earnings growth at Korean memory-chip makers came from higher memory-chip prices. By contrast, TSMC and Japanese chip-equipment makers relied more on advanced manufacturing and process expertise, giving them more durable growth prospects, they added.
Taiwan's Taiex has climbed about 7% in the second half of the year, taking its year-to-date gains to about 70% as investors broaden their bets across the AI hardware supply chain.
South Korea's rally was driven largely by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose soaring memory-chip profits made them among the biggest winners of the AI boom. Together, the companies account for more than half of the Kospi, leaving the market unusually dependent on a single segment of the semiconductor industry.
Even blockbuster earnings are no longer enough to excite investors. Last Thursday, Samsung forecast a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, yet its shares have fallen for two straight trading sessions.
The reversal followed months of extraordinary volatility. The Kospi plunged 22% in July, its worst month since the 2008 financial crisis, before rebounding 18% on the month's final trading day for its biggest one-day gain on record. The swings triggered multiple market-wide circuit breakers as leveraged bets on chip stocks amplified the moves.
Young South Koreans flooded social media with memes and dark humor about their battered portfolios, while regulators tightened rules on leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds after concerns the products had fueled speculation.
Trading has cooled sharply. Turnover has dropped 70% from its late-May peak, while foreign investors have continued pulling money from Korean equities.
The shift didn't happen overnight.
Even before Korea's selloff, investors were debating whether the next phase of the AI boom would continue rewarding memory-chip makers or broaden to companies with exposure across the semiconductor supply chain.
Taiwan appears to be benefiting from that shift. Its market offers exposure across AI infrastructure, from advanced chip manufacturing and packaging to servers and networking equipment.
That includes TSMC as well as companies involved in advanced packaging, servers, networking equipment, and other AI infrastructure.
The Taiex outperformed the Kospi by more than 23 percentage points in the third quarter, as Taiwan's benchmark gained nearly 4% while South Korea's plunged more than 19%.

articles.title_orig: EU adopts nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia
articles.title_zh: EU adopts nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia
articles.content_orig:
German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.
"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.
"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilities ahead of winter.
US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.
