articles.title_orig: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
articles.title_zh: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.
Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.
This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.
Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.
Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

articles.title_orig: China's debt interest costs are soaring—and growing faster than any other major budget category
articles.title_zh: China's debt interest costs are soaring—and growing faster than any other major budget category
articles.content_orig:
The world is flooded with debt, but while the U.S. and Europe have caused angst on global markets lately, China’s fiscal situation isn’t looking so great either.
In fact, China’s debt has shot up so much in recent years that interest payments on all its borrowing are commanding a bigger share of public spending.
Debt-servicing payments will account for 19.2% of the central government’s general public budget this year, up from 12% in 2014, according to new Conference Board estimates cited by the Financial Times .
That tracks with a separate report earlier this year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies , which also found that 19% of Beijing’s spending is earmarked for interest on debt. That’s more than the 14% of the U.S. federal budget that goes to interest costs, though less than Japan’s 25.6%.
CSIS added that China’s spending on interest payments skyrocketed 341% between 2013 and 2025, faster than any other major budget category. By comparison, total spending jumped 102% in that span, with outlays on social security and employment up 207%, science and technology up 137%, and defense up 141%.
To be sure, U.S. debt-interest spending looks grim too and has surged about 390% since 2013 to $1 trillion, which also tops the Pentagon’s budget.
But the world’s two biggest economies have been diverging in key ways with implications for future growth and indebtedness.
The U.S. economy is accelerating, helped by the AI boom, and despite high inflation, resilient consumers have continued to spend. Unemployment is low and signals full employment, while stock markets are at or near record highs.
Of course, hyperscalers are racing to issue bonds to fund their data centers and chip purchases, but they are also raising money with fresh stock offerings and IPOs.
Meanwhile, China’s GDP has been decelerating and is on pace to undercut its annual target of 4.5%-5%. And while export-facing sectors are growing at a fast clip, trade partners are putting up barriers, Chinese consumers remain reluctant to spend, investment is weak, the property sector is still digging out from an epic crash, and Chinese stocks have been anemic.
Beijing has also steered state banks to provide financing to priority industries like electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence and renewable energy.
But under pressure to lend, many loans went to questionable borrowers. Business debt has doubled since 2019, while revenues are only 30% higher. Creditors continue to roll over loans to keep struggling firms afloat, even as nearly a third of them are losing money.
China’s state-led growth model now looks like it’s running out of steam, and the rapidly expanding mountain of debt is a warning sign as local governments often seek to boost favored industries with low-cost loans.
According to the International Monetary Fund , China’s general government gross debt hit 107% of GDP this year, up from 41% in 2015 and on a path to reach 124% in 2030.
A broader measure of indebtedness across the public and private sectors reveals an even worse picture. China’s total debt-to-GDP ratio, excluding the financial sector, doubled since 2010 and has now topped 300%, Capital Economics estimated earlier this year.
But in the U.S., total public and private debt last year was about 265% of GDP, down sharply from pandemic-era highs.
Not only has China’s debt boom hit diminishing returns, but it’s also becoming a drag on the economy.
“The irony is that one driver of both government borrowing and the lax lending standards of [state-owned] banks is the desire to prop up economic growth and prevent job losses,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, wrote in May. “But the product of a credit boom that has been underway for 18 years is a banking system propping up unproductive firms, widespread losses across industry, and entrenched overcapacity.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Bishops around the world ask for prayers for Pope Leo XIV’s health
articles.title_zh: Bishops around the world ask for prayers for Pope Leo XIV’s health
articles.content_orig:
Prayers for the pope’s health have been pouring in from all over the world.
Bishops from around the world asked for prayers for Pope Leo XIV after he announced on Sunday, Oct. 11, that he will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on one of his lungs in the coming days.
In the United States, Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. bishops’ conference, said the prelates would join “the faithful and all people of good will in praying for his good health.” He also prayed for those who will perform the operation: “May the hand of Pope Leo’s surgeons be guided by the divine physician, Jesus Christ.”
Archbishop Ronald Hicks of New York joined the prayers as he finished a week-long pilgrimage on the Camino de Santiago in Spain. “I join with the bishops, priests, faithful, and all people of good will of the Archdiocese of New York in praying for our Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, as he prepares for his surgery later this week,” he wrote . He also asked Jesus, “the divine physician,” to care for the pope and guide “the hands of his surgeons, nurses, and other health professionals.”
Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, also wrote about the news. Uruguay is one of the countries expecting Pope Leo XIV on his upcoming visit to Latin America. “Let us pray for his speedy recovery and continue with greater spirit the preparation for his visit to our land,” he wrote.
In Peru, which also expects the pope later this year, the Archdiocese of Lima entrusted his health to the Lord of Miracles, a devotion that draws millions of Peruvians each year. “We ask the Lord of Miracles for his speedy recovery,” the archdiocese said on social media.
The Peruvian bishops’ conference issued a message titled “United in prayer for the health of the Holy Father Leo XIV.” It noted the :serenity and humility” with which the pope shared the news and asked that his health be entrusted to the Lord of Miracles.
“Lifting to God, Lord of life and source of all health, our supplications that he strengthen him and grant him the health that the fulfillment of his mission requires,” the Peruvian bishops said. They also urged communities, families, and the faithful to place the Holy Father under the maternal protection of the Blessed Virgin Mary, so that in the fullness of his strength he may continue his mission in service of the Church and all humanity, as a messenger of peace and hope and a witness of unity, fraternity, and encounter among all peoples.
The Argentinian bishops said in a statement: “We ask the Lord to grant him strength and peace at this time, that the operation may go well, and that he may make a swift and full recovery.”
The Spanish bishops’ conference also invited prayer for the pope. Its president, Archbishop Luis Argüello, asked “the whole Spanish Church — dioceses, institutes of consecrated life, communities and lay associations, all members of the People of God, and our fellow citizens — to pray for the health of our beloved Pope Leo XIV.”
The conference’s secretary general, Bishop Francisco César García Magán, recalled the welcome Leo XIV received on his recent visit to Spain and said the faithful can now show him their closeness in another way: “Now we show it by uniting in prayer.”
The conference’s secretary general, Bishop Francisco César García Magán, recalled the welcome Leo XIV received on his recent visit to Spain and said the faithful can now show him their closeness in another way: “Now we show it by uniting in prayer.”
Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda, the president of the Polish Bishops’ Conference, issued an appeal to the Polish people, asking them to “pray for the Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, asking God for a successful operation and a speedy recovery.”
Bishop John Keenan, on behalf of the Scottish bishops’ conference, said : “We invite Catholics across Scotland, and all people of goodwill, to join us in praying for Pope Leo, for the medical team caring for him, and for a successful operation and a full and speedy recovery.”
Archbishop Richard Moth of Westminster and the president of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales, assured Leo of the prayers of the faithful.
“We pray that following the procedure and a period of recovery, he will soon be restored to health,” Moth wrote.
Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Archbishop of Malta and Adjunct Secretary of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, wrote on X : “The Church in Malta is united in prayer for the Holy Father, wishing him well for the surgery he will be undergoing.”
The pope announced the operation after Sunday’s Angelus. Doctors found a nodule on one of his lungs and recommended removing it. In sharing the news, Leo asked the faithful to accompany him spiritually in the coming days: “I entrust myself to your prayer.”
This story was first published by ACI Prensa, the Spanish-language sister service of EWTN News. It has been translated and adapted by EWTN News English.

articles.title_orig: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
articles.title_zh: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday that President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia to allow it to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis said.
Trump announced Friday on Truth Social that Russia would “immediately supply” hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the global marketplace, with more than 1 million additional tons soon on the way. The move drew sharp condemnation from Ukraine and critics of the Trump administration.
Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, lawmakers took a series of steps to try to financially punish the Kremlin. In 2022, the Senate unanimously passed a bill to ban Russian oil imports, and Congress has not changed the law to reflect Trump’s announcement.
Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether he believes Trump is breaking the law with his Russia deal, Tillis said, “I believe that he may be.”
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor,” he added. “Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tillis’ remarks.
Tillis referred to year-end congressional funding negotiations when he was asked what the Senate could do if he believes Trump is breaking the law.
“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” he said.
Asked whether Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin was putting American lives at risk, Tillis said, “It absolutely will,” pointing to Russian funding of mercenaries and the Kremlin’s relationship with Iran.
Tillis has just months left before his term expires. His retirement from the Senate created a high-profile battleground opening. Democrats are eyeing his seat as a prime target to flip as they seek control of the chamber.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., voted against the Russia sanction bill in 2022, and he backed Trump’s decision. Massie said Sunday on X that he voted against the sanctions because they would lead to higher prices in the U.S.
“Glad to see Trump came around to that reality this week,” Massie said in the post. “We should lift sanctions on all petroleum products, and on raw metals like copper and aluminum.”
Massie has frequently criticized Trump during the second Trump administration, and he lost his re-election bid to a Trump-backed challenger.
Tillis, too, has been highly critical of aspects of the Trump administration, including the performance of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Tillis, who voted for Hegseth’s confirmation, now says he regrets his vote.
Tillis on Sunday condemned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas.
Tillis said the livestream plans would radicalize people and be used by terrorist groups as a recruiting tool.
“The Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life,” he said.
“This is not who we are, and it’s another example of why Pete Hegseth, in all of his bravado, needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader, and we need strong leadership supporting President Trump right now,” he added.
Megan Brand is a politics reporter for NBC News.
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Passenger terminal at Riyadh airport is struck again, a day after 12 were killed
articles.title_zh: Passenger terminal at Riyadh airport is struck again, a day after 12 were killed
articles.content_orig:
This image from video obtained and verified by AP shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (UGC via AP) AP/UGC hide caption
CAIRO — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday.
The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.
On Sunday, the Houthis also claimed attacks on King Fahd Airport in the city of Damma, as well as oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday.
The rebels again warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces." Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the group's military spokesperson, wrote on X that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, however, were exempt. The kingdom earlier called Mecca a "red line."
A Saudi statement said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, who worked for Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran's most powerful allies. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The Houthis say they have now imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains near the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
But Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire. "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign," he said.
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias’ devastating aftermath comes into focus in striking images
articles.content_orig:
United Cajun Navy Incident Cmdr. Josh Gill joins ‘Fox News Live’ as Florida communities begin cleaning up after Hurricane Isaias left widespread damage and power outages in its wake. Gill discusses recovery efforts on the ground and how volunteers are helping residents clear debris and rebuild after the storm.
Communities are beginning to assess the damage left behind by a powerful hurricane that tore through the region, leaving homes damaged, roads flooded and neighborhoods littered with debris.
Photos from some of the hardest-hit areas show the scale of the destruction as residents and emergency crews begin the long process of cleaning up and rebuilding.
HOW THE VIOLENT CATEGORY 2 STORM UNFOLDED ACROSS FLORIDA AND GULF COAST
Copper Brock helps salvage what he can from the Milton Quick Stop after the roof was torn off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Isaias slammed into the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, bringing destructive winds, dangerous storm surge and widespread flooding.
The hurricane tore roofs from buildings, uprooted trees and knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of customers across Florida and Alabama before pushing inland.
STUNNING FOOTAGE CAPTURES HURRICANE ISAIAS FROM INSIDE THE STORM’S EYE
In an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with category two winds. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Isaias marked the first hurricane to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast since Hurricane Milton battered Florida in October 2024, nearly two years earlier.
The storm also became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, ending an unusually quiet stretch that saw no hurricanes develop until October.
DESANTIS DEPLOYS AN ARMY TO CLEAR ROADS, RESTORE POWER AFTER ISAIAS' LANDFALL

As Isaias moved inland and weakened, the full extent of the hurricane's destruction began to emerge.
Stunning images from across the Gulf Coast capture what the powerful storm left behind.

articles.title_orig: Man dies after entering tiger habitat at British zoo
articles.title_zh: Man dies after entering tiger habitat at British zoo
articles.content_orig:
Ed Miliband, whose constituency includes the park, offers ‘deepest condolences’ to family of visitor who entered enclosure on Saturday
A wildlife park in Yorkshire has confirmed the tiger that mauled to death a man who entered its enclosure will not be euthanised.
A man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering a tiger enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, located near Doncaster , before police were called at 1.35pm on Saturday.
South Yorkshire police said the tiger “subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury” and despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.
In a statement on Sunday, the wildlife park thanked those who had expressed concern after the “tragic incident” and said their “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” remained with the family of the man who lost his life.
“The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support,” the statement read. The park also confirmed that the tiger, named Altai, was “safe and well and will not be euthanised” after the incident.
The foreign secretary and MP for Doncaster North, Ed Miliband , said he was “deeply saddened” and sent his “thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died”.
“I am very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded,” Miliband added.
One visitor at the park, Marie Miller, wrote in a Facebook post that she had seen the man before the incident and he was “happily enjoying” his visit. Miller said the man had asked a stranger to take a picture of him.
“The man who I saw on the bridge with his earpods in dancing was happily enjoying seeing the tiger,” the post read.
“He asked a total stranger to take a picture of him with the tiger in the background.”
Another visitor, who did not want to be identified, told the South West News Service that it was “frightening and confusing” when the park was evacuated after the incident.
She said: “At first, we were all scared and confused because we had no idea what was going on. Different routes had been closed off, and staff were positioned around the park directing visitors where to go.
“The scariest part was not knowing what was happening.”
The visitor said she heard people saying the man was 22, but was unable to confirm this. “As we walked past the police near the tiger enclosure, we saw officers surrounding a young man in the tiger enclosure,” she said. “We saw an air ambulance outside the park, although, from what we observed, it didn’t take anyone away.”
South Yorkshire police said the man’s family was made aware of the incident on Saturday and were being supported by specialist officers. The force has encouraged people not to share videos of the incident that have been circulating online.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is on a purpose-built 2-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.

articles.title_orig: Xi Focus: Xi leads efforts toward building Healthy China
articles.title_zh: Xi Focus: Xi leads efforts toward building Healthy China
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- On a small island in the Yangtze River in eastern China, residents don't need to leave the island to see a medical specialist. They can now access modern medical equipment at the township clinic and consult specialists from higher-level hospitals, who pay regular visits to the facility.
In December 2014, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the clinic in Shiye Township, Jiangsu Province, outlining a path for advancing rural healthcare. Shiye is home to five villages and more than 10,000 permanent residents.
"We must shift the focus of healthcare to the community level, channel more medical resources to local communities, and promote equal access to basic public services in urban and rural areas," said Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission.
This is to provide people with safe, effective, accessible and affordable public health services and basic medical care, and effectively address the difficulties and high costs people face in accessing medical care at the local level, he added.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in late 2012, the Party Central Committee, with Xi at the core, has given strategic priority to ensuring people's health. It made the major decision to advance the Healthy China Initiative nationwide.
From targeted advances in key areas to nationwide coverage of inclusive health services that meet basic needs, China, a country of more than 1.4 billion people, has blazed a path of inclusive and balanced health development.
Over the years, Xi has visited grassroots medical institutions and households in rural areas across the country, offering targeted guidance tailored to local conditions.
He has focused on preventing people from falling into or returning to poverty because of illness, using remote consultations to help balance medical resources, and addressing healthcare-related issues in rural areas.
Xi has paid close attention to the issues people face in accessing healthcare at the grassroots level and set out clear directions, from establishing five basic systems -- tiered diagnosis and treatment, modern hospital management, universal medical insurance, drug supply security, and comprehensive oversight -- to developing the healthcare workforce and digital infrastructure for smart healthcare.
"We must unswervingly uphold the public welfare nature of the medical and healthcare sector, and not take the path of wholesale marketization and commercialization," Xi said.
He has also called for further deepening the reform of medical and healthcare systems and exploring Chinese solutions to the worldwide challenge of healthcare reform.
Coordinated development and governance of healthcare services, medical insurance and pharmaceuticals have helped reduce out-of-pocket payments to 27.1 percent of total health expenditure.
The vision of ensuring that serious illnesses can be treated within one's province, common illnesses within one's city or county, and everyday ailments at the grassroots level is increasingly becoming a reality.
China has supported the development of 125 national regional medical centers so far, with 75 percent of their hospitals located in central and western regions and other areas where high-quality medical resources are relatively scarce.
More than 90 percent of residents can access nearby medical and healthcare services within 15 minutes. Primary-level medical institutions account for more than 50 percent of all medical visits nationwide.
COMPREHENSIVE LIFECYCLE HEALTH
Xi has also expressed deep concern over the growing prevalence of myopia among students, particularly at younger ages.
The trend, he has said, seriously affects children's health and poses a major issue for the future of the country, and it must be given high priority and not allowed to continue unchecked.
With strengthened efforts to prevent and control myopia among children and adolescents, China's overall student myopia rate declined for five consecutive years from 2021 to 2025, reaching 49.9 percent in 2025, down 3.7 percentage points from 2018.
From enabling older people to enjoy their later years to preventing childhood obesity and myopia, Xi has stressed the importance of safeguarding health across all population groups and throughout the entire lifecycle.
A range of health indicators point to improvements in the country's overall health status.
In 2025, China's average life expectancy rose to 79.25 years, while its major health indicators remained at the leading position among upper-middle-income countries and countries with a population exceeding 100 million. The premature mortality rate from major chronic diseases fell to 13.8 percent, and major infectious diseases and endemic diseases were brought under effective control.
China aims to establish a health system by 2035 that is compatible with a society that has basically achieved modernization.
Xi has emphasized the translation of scientific and technological innovations into practical applications, called for advancing the digital and intelligent development of healthcare nationwide, and encouraged regions with suitable conditions to explore the application of artificial intelligence.
This year, the government work report included biomedicine as an emerging pillar industry for the first time.
In the first half of 2026 alone, China approved 38 innovative drugs for market entry.
China is developing a growing range of homegrown drugs, medical equipment, vaccines, medical consumables and approaches to diagnosis and treatment.
Traditional Chinese medicine is a distinctive component of China's healthcare system. Xi has issued important instructions on multiple occasions, calling for the sector's industrial development and modernization, as well as wider international reach.
China has also continued to deepen health cooperation with countries around the world by promoting the use of artemisinin to benefit patients worldwide, regularly deploying medical teams abroad, establishing overseas traditional Chinese medicine centers, and joining efforts to combat Ebola. Through these efforts, it has worked with other countries to address cross-border public health risks.
Yet as China's economy and society evolve and its demographic landscape changes, people's healthcare needs are becoming increasingly multi-layered and diverse.
"At present and for a period to come, China's health and healthcare work needs to adapt to changing circumstances and refine certain specific policies and measures. However, the path of health and healthcare development with Chinese characteristics must not waver," Xi said. ■

articles.content_orig:
On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:
Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.
And this week on Face the Nation: President Trump scrambles to cut last- minute deals ahead of the midterms, the latest prompting backlash within his own party. Twenty-three days to go before the votes are counted, and the atypical campaign continues.
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's a good question. The answer? Making sure his loyalists get out and vote Republican. Late Friday, Trump cut a deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel in an effort to lower the price of fuel in America.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: He's freeing up a lot of oil for the world, OK? That's a good thing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But will Trump's deal with Putin prompt even more Republican candidates to distance themselves from him?
We will ask the number two in the Senate, Wyoming Republican John Barrasso.
Democrats have their own challenges. How are they going to get their loyalists to turn out? We will talk with Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy and the Democratic nominee for Senate in New Hampshire Congressman Chris Pappas.
Then: ICE deportation tactics are back in the spotlight following an ICE- involved shooting in New York City. We will get the latest on that and an update on the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
Finally, another view on AI with the chief technology officer at Palantir, Shyam Sankar.
It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.
We've got a lot of politics ahead, but we want to start with a quick update on the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall Friday night and resulted in the deaths of four people.
For that update, we turn to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
Good morning to you, Mr. Secretary.
This is the first Atlantic hurricane of the year, hundreds of thousands of people left without power. I know the president approves some federal support. What is needed?
MARKWAYNE MULLIN (U.S. Homeland Security Secretary): Well, we – we're in touch with the – with all the governors that are affected and might be affected by the continuing storm moving across the nation.
The president has been very involved in this from the get-go. Cam Hamilton, who is our director of FEMA, we started prepositioning assets into every state and working closely with their emergency responders.
Right now, from the conversation I have had with each governor, they're in good shape. We're – we have good partnership. What's interesting about this area is, they're – while they may not have been hit with storms real bad the last two years, they work really, really good together.
When I was talking to Governor Kemp from – you know, from Georgia, he was talking about his relationship with Ron DeSantis. When we're dealing with the other governors, they were talking about how they're cooperating with sending assets to the areas that are affected without power to get the – the power restored.
FEMA is standing by, responding with – with lifesaving responses. The Coast Guard is out in the inner waters and the Mississippi, the mouth of Mississippi, out in the – our shores. And we are still doing some boat rescues, but, really, it's more recovery of the boats, not of the individuals.
So we're working together well as a team. We were – you know, you never can be fully prepared for – for a storm like this, but I can tell you that the coordination from – from the Oval Office with President Trump's leadership to the – to the governors to the county first responders…
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: … we're all working very closely together.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we hope everyone in that pathway is safe.
I want to ask you about something else on the enforcement side of things. There have been at least 30 DHS officer-involved shootings under the Trump administration, according to CBS's tally of events here. There was this incident last week in New York City.
And the NYPD did release security video that shows a man dressed as a civilian with a gun drawn approaching a car and then punching in the window. I know you have said there were other DHS ICE officers in the area who were put at risk by the driver.
But just to clarify events, when are you going to release the body cameras worn by those officers?
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: Well, Margaret, what you're seeing is a pole cam.
What you're not seeing is actual – the audio footage or a different angle, where you have multiple officers that are actually approaching this – this individual named Oscar with a long, very long, extensive rap sheet.
He's only been in the country for – for three years, and he has a rap sheet of four charges of felony robbery, two charges of felony assault, felony larceny, misdemeanor assault, possession of – of weapons, possession of stolen property, two felony charges of drugless – of dangerous drugs, and strong gang affiliation that – that has direct or indirect knowledge of – of a CBP officer that was shot last year.
And this guy evaded officers last month when we tried to get to him.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: We knew he was armed. We knew he was dangerous. We knew – or there was a possibility of him being armed. We knew he was dangerous, and we knew he was going to evade.
So when we approached his vehicle, we were giving lawful commands. We had approached him just like any other undercover agency that's out there from local, state, federal or – or county that has undercover officers. We had our badges out, once again, giving lawful demands.
He decided that he was going to accelerate and try to evade again. We had taken every precaution to try to keep that from happening, and – and, unfortunately, this took place.
We would have loved for him to exit the vehicle like we asked him to. He decided not to. And, unfortunately, because of the selfish behavior, he put his 5-year-old at danger. But as far as…
MARGARET BRENNAN: You said they were wearing body cameras. Will…
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: … the information being released…
MARGARET BRENNAN: When will you release that footage?
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: As far – Margaret, as far as the information being released, FBI and HSI is going to do the investigation, continue to do the investigation. When it's completed, we'll release all the information.
There was that 5-year-old you just mentioned. Given that rap sheet and how long you'd been monitoring, how come those officers didn't notice that a child was put in that car?
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: Well, what our understanding is, is, he drove into the neighborhood.
We knew his pattern of life, but we didn't know the 5-year-old was in the vehicle. Who did know who the 5 – who was in the vehicle was Oscar. Now, as a father of six individuals – or six kids, I mean…
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: … no way would I ever put my kids in danger. If I was getting lawful commands – and he knew he was being sought after. He knew the police was looking for him because, like I said, he just evaded a month ago.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: I would have immediately got out of my vehicle to protect my – my – my child.
There's no way I would have been selfish enough to put my child in danger.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: He was absolutely selfish enough to put his child in danger. He's the one that decided to accelerate and – and ram into another vehicle with his 5-year-old in the vehicle, and then tried to accelerate towards other police officers.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: That's – that is – that tells you the type of character that Oscar is. And yet somehow the mayor is out there protesting about this.
SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: But yet, seven days ago, when an NYPD officer got stabbed in the same neighborhood by – by criminals t

The mic would let users control the set-top box using Siri without having to speak into the remote or a connected HomePod device. If you happen to misplace the remote, the new integrated speaker should make it easier to track down. It could play an audio alert to guide you to its location, whether it got carelessly kicked under the couch or a child mischievously hid it in a drawer.

articles.title_zh: The original Apple TV 4K from 2017 is now officially "vintage" - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
The smart streaming box/stick market is a bit weird for sure. There are all sorts of options out there, but each with distinct problems and limitations. Generic Android boxes are plentiful and can be powerful, but often offer a suboptimal software experience and format and technology support. There are cheap and easily available reputable options out there like Amazon's Firestick line, though that might be getting even more locked down with the move to Vega OS. Walmart has its "onn" line, but it is kind of US-only. Anyone actually serious about this device either swears by the Nvidia Shield TV Pro, dating back to 2019 or an Apple TV. The latter does have more recent iterations, like the 3rd-generation Apple TV 4K from 2022.
We already know that Apple is gearing up to unveil a whole bunch of new smart home devices on October 13 and apparently that will include at least one Apple TV device. This has been rumored already but is now further confirmed by the fact that Apple recently relegated the original Apple TV 4K from 2017 as a "vintage" device. In Apple vernacular, "vintage" means over five years have passed since a product stopped being available for sale, while there is also "obsolete", which means over seven years have passed since sales discontinued. Obsolete devices are pretty much impossible to service officially, while vintage ones are difficult, but still possible.
What does that mean if you own a 2017 Apple TV 4K? Most likely you will be able to continue using it just fine if it meets your needs and if it is working properly, that is. If the latter is not true and you have one sitting in a drawer for some reason, you might want to get it to an Apple service center soon. Or, of course, you could just wait and get whatever new Apple TV is released in a few days.
It was supported for 9 years with tvOS 26.6 from July 2026 being its last software update. Apple TV HD from 2015 also has the same last software update and that one was kept alive for nearly 11 years.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin drives a wedge through the Western alliance
articles.title_zh: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin drives a wedge through the Western alliance
articles.content_orig:
By agreeing to open Russia’s taps and release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into a starving global market, the Kremlin has achieved something that raw military might on the battlefields of eastern Ukraine could never deliver.
The deal, which involves suspending fuel export sanctions on Russia for six months to allow for diesel sales at market prices, will be a welcome boon for a Russian economy that is creaking under the strain of a war in Ukraine that has dragged on far longer than anticipated.
But for Vladimir Putin, Russia’s strongman president, the real benefit isn’t the billions of dollars in fresh revenue. It is the wedge this deal, and the rhetoric around it, drives right through the heart of the Western alliance, which has aimed to isolate Moscow over it’s war in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump spelled out the new and extraordinary reality in stark terms as he mocked the angry reaction of Ukraine’s wartime leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, who derided the deal as a “weak decision by a strong partner” that provides “extra money for this war.”
“We said you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused and he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers,” Trump said before calling for a new Ukrainian leader, essentially blaming high global fuel prices, especially acute in the United States, on Ukraine.
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney sided with Zelensky as the two leaders spoke on Sunday, saying that the agreement stands “in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.”
In recent months, relentless Ukrainian drone strikes, flying deep into Russian territory with terrifying precision, have systematically crippled oil refineries that serve as both the economic engine and the fuel tank for Russia’s military.
Amid domestic fuel shortages and severe production cuts, the Kremlin suspended all diesel exports this month so that it had enough for its own needs — a stunning setback for a country that used to be the second-biggest diesel exporter in the world before the Ukraine war.
Whether Russia can actually provide the promised diesel or not, by framing the Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries as an assault on American interests, Washington is effectively aligning its economic priorities with Moscow’s survival — even as analysts have suggested the deal is unlikely to dramatically move the needle on diesel prices.
The US has powerful levers it can pull to get Ukraine to play ball.
Washington no longer provides money and weapons to Kyiv. But vital American intelligence sharing — the digital backbone of Ukrainian defense — risks being cut off if Ukraine now continues to strike at the Russian infrastructure Trump wants left untouched. The threat is real — the US did just that in the wake of the notorious Oval Office blowup last year.
Mindful of the risk , Zelensky has indicated he is willing to cooperate, but only if Russia does the same. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said in a recent statement.
For Ukraine, this entire episode may seem like yet another bitter, existential betrayal by an American leader who has at times acknowledged a begrudging respect for Kyiv’s bold military tactics. Now, its most effective asymmetric weapon — relentless drone strikes on oil refineries — is being undermined and may be neutralized, not by Russian anti-air batteries, but by American diplomatic pressure along with Trump’s irrepressible urge to do a deal with the Kremlin.
In Moscow, on the other hand, the mood is upbeat.
“The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large,” Putin said in an official statement after a prearranged telephone call with Trump on Friday night.
“I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” he added.
Privately, the Kremlin leader must be rubbing his hands with glee.
Both he and Trump want Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries to immediately stop.
Both want Ukraine’s president to be replaced with someone who will agree a quick deal.
And just a few weeks after Trump signed a bill into law, sponsored by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, allowing for punishing sanctions to be imposed on any country that bought Russian oil, Washington has now become a customer itself.
All at once, it seems, a battered but relatively unified Western front that has stood against resource-rich Moscow for more than four years looks like it is being dealt another powerful blow.

articles.title_orig: Some California beaches forced to close after 'unusually high' ocean water levels from Tropical Storm Rachel - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Some California beaches forced to close after 'unusually high' ocean water levels from Tropical Storm Rachel - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
All beaches and piers in Newport Beach, California, are closed, officials said.
The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel , along with a separate storm system over the Western United States, continued to sweep across the West on Sunday, fueling flooding in several Southern California coastal communities.
Post-Tropical Storm Rachel made landfall in Baja California Saturday night, but as it moved in, its impact was already being felt along the West Coast.
A combination of large ocean swells stirred up by Rachel and prolonged swells due in part to an El Niño-enhanced Kelvin wave has produced major flooding along Southern California's coast.
One of the hardest-hit areas has been Newport Beach in Orange County, which has been experiencing flooding since Friday.
Main drags like Balboa Boulevard in Newport Beach and numerous adjacent streets have been drenched in floodwaters.
The City of Newport Beach declared a local emergency on Saturday in response to the flooding caused by Tropical Storm Rachel.
"This declaration will help the City secure additional resources as crews continue working to protect homes, property and public safety," the city said in a statement on Saturday, adding that elevated surf and "unusually high ocean water levels" are expected to continue through the weekend, with the highest tides anticipated Sunday.
All of the city beaches and piers in Newport Beach are closed until further notice, the city said.
"Stay away from these areas. Flooding and hazardous conditions pose serious safety risks," the city advised residents in its statement.
Tropical Storm Rachel became post-tropical late Saturday night about 80 miles south-southeast of San Diego. However, its remnants and the separate system over the West will continue to fuel a flash flood threat across portions of the Southwest, as well as bring rough surf and gusty winds, on Sunday and into Monday.
The flash flood threat is expected to continue to unfold on Sunday, with the greatest risk to parts of Southern California, northwest Arizona, southern Nevada, and southwest Utah, where a level 3 of 4 threat for flash flooding is in place.
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for Orange County beaches that starts at 3 p.m. on Sunday and continues through Tuesday afternoon, warning of potentially significant flooding and beach erosion fueled in part by Tropical Storm Rachel's remnants.
The greatest concern is high tide through Sunday morning and swells from the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel could create dangerous conditions with beach erosion and seawater once again flooding beach roads and paths.
Other cities along the Southern California coast -- including Laguna Beach, Huntington Beach and San Clemente -- were distributing sandbags to the public on Sunday in preparation for possible flooding.
In Seal Beach, about 30 miles south of Los Angeles, police reported that "due to elevated surf and coastal flooding concerns" beach parking lots were being closed on Sunday "as a precaution to protect life and property."
On Saturday, the outer bands from Tropical Storm Rachel brought gusty winds and heavy rain to parts of Southern California and Arizona.
Wind gusts of over 60 mph were reported during thunderstorms that hit Menifee and Temecula, California. Heavy rain of up to 1 to 2 inches was reported with these storms as well, causing isolated instances of flash flooding and debris flow.
Gusty winds also produced a dust storm near Phoenix, Arizona, on Saturday with near-zero visibility reported.

articles.title_orig: The Citroën 2CV Is Back As An Ultra-Affordable City Car
articles.title_zh: The Citroën 2CV Is Back As An Ultra-Affordable City Car
articles.content_orig:
Fiat set the template with the 500, and Renault followed with the latest Twingo. Now, Citroën wants in on the retro city-car revival with a modern take on one of France’s most recognizable cars: the 2CV .
Known affectionately as the "Duck," or "La Deuche" in France, the 2CV is making a comeback at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. And judging by the concept, Citroën isn't simply trying to copy the original.
Citroën's goal was to create a small EV that's practical and inexpensive, but something that still feels special to drive. The production car would slot between the tiny Ami and the C3 in Citroën's lineup.
Despite its modern technology, the 2CV Concept is actually smaller than the original. It measures about 147.6 inches (3.7 meters) long, compared to the roughly 151.2 inches (3.8 meters) of the original 2CV.
Citroën says keeping the dimensions compact was intentional. The idea was to bring back the light, playful nature of small cars while making the vehicle easy to drive and park in crowded cities.
The target weight is around 2,200 pounds, too. Keeping the car light means Citroën doesn't need an enormous battery to provide useful everyday range. That should also help keep the purchase price and running costs down.
The concept takes the same minimalist approach to its construction. Broad, flat body panels, simple air intakes below the windshield, and separate bumpers that can be replaced individually are all designed to make the car easier and cheaper to build and repair.
Citroën is also working with Michelin on a “universal digital tire twin,” which is designed to monitor tire health and continuously adapt the vehicle's behavior based on road and environmental conditions.
The design is where the connection to the original 2CV is most obvious. The concept has the same basic proportions and rounded silhouette, but Citroën has tightened up the details for the modern era. There's a steep windshield, a gently curved roof, prominent fenders, and relatively simple body surfacing.
Up front are freestanding round headlights paired with a modern LED light signature. The hood also incorporates a reference to the historic TPV project—the “Toute Petite Voiture,” or “very small car”—that eventually became the 2CV.
There are also some deliberately old-school touches, including exposed windshield wipers and air openings integrated into the front end.
From the side, the concept gets more playful. The door handles take inspiration from the original 2CV, while slim turn signals sit in the rear roof pillars. The 19-inch steel wheels are another modern interpretation of a classic design.
The rear is arguably the most distinctive part of the car, with a curved roofline, black tailgate extending down into the bumper, and horizontal LED lighting elements. Even the license plate is a little Easter egg, with the various nicknames given to the 2CV around the world.
Citroën isn't trying to turn the 2CV into another screen-filled EV, either.
The interior is bright and open, with wide seats featuring the company's Advanced Comfort technology. The passenger seat can slide outward, while removable storage baskets and soft strap-style door handles add some useful practicality.
Instead of a conventional dashboard, the driver gets a minimalist control setup centered around a cylindrical structure. It houses the steering wheel, control stalks, shift paddle, and Citroën Smart Vision Display, which projects important information into the driver's line of sight.
There's also an 8.0-inch square touchscreen that combines digital functions with physical controls. Its graphics are inspired by comic books, adding a little personality to what could otherwise be a very basic interface.
Then there's “Radioën,” a removable radio that doubles as a portable speaker. You can take it out of the car and bring the music with you, which is neat.
A fabric folding roof is another obvious nod to the original 2CV, giving the cabin a more open and airy feel. The elaborate string of lights around the interior, however, probably isn't making the transition to production.
The 2CV Concept is filled with tons of little references to the original. The exterior is finished in a color called “Infra Red,” combining orange, yellow, and red tones as a nod to the classic 2CV Spot. Inside, the seats feature a modern take on the old 2CV's checkered upholstery.
There are also beige Bakelite-inspired elements throughout the cabin. Bakelite was one of the first fully synthetic plastics and was used for various components on early 2CVs. Wood, textured fabrics, wicker-inspired materials, and 3D-printed storage baskets give the interior a warmer, more tactile feel than the typical modern EV cabin.
Even the pedals get in on the joke; a turtle represents the brake, while a hare marks the accelerator.
The door pockets are another clever callback. They're designed to carry eggs, referencing one of the famous requirements from the original 2CV's development brief. The horn and electric motor sounds reference the original car, while the ventilation flaps beneath the windshield and umbrella-handle-style selector mimic familiar 2CV details.
The numbers 48, 90, and 26 on the windshield represent the original car's launch year, the end of its production run, and the year of this concept's debut.
Citroën says the production version will be built in Europe and is targeting a starting price of around €15,000 (or around $16,000 at current conversion rates). That would make it one of the more affordable ways to get into an electric car, assuming Citroën can keep the final price anywhere close to that target.
The production model is expected to arrive by 2028, potentially making its debut at the 2028 Paris Motor Show. If that happens, the timing would be perfect: exactly 80 years after the original 2CV first appeared.
Of course, not everything on this concept will survive the trip to production, but if Citroën can preserve the basic formula—a lightweight, inexpensive, practical EV with plenty of personality—the 2CV could be one of the more interesting entries in Europe's growing crop of affordable electric city cars.

articles.title_orig: Taste Test: Maker’s Mark Nailed Its First Mizunara-Finished Bourbon
articles.title_zh: Taste Test: Maker’s Mark Nailed Its First Mizunara-Finished Bourbon
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to Taste Test , where every week our critic Jonah Flicker explores the most buzzworthy and interesting whiskeys in the world. Check back each Sunday for his latest whiskey review .
It seems like there are only a few brands and distilleries left that haven’t yet used Japanese mizunara oak to age their bourbon . Maker’s Mark was one of these, at least until now—the new World Wood Collection Expedition 01 marks the first time that this Kentucky distillery has given its bourbon a mizunara finish. Of course, true to form, this was done with wood staves and not secondary barrels, and I’m happy to report that the result is one of the best and most interesting releases in Maker’s Wood Finishing series to date.
Over the 60 years and change that it’s been making whiskey , Maker’s Mark has been distilling wheated bourbon, meaning bourbon that is made using wheat instead of rye as the secondary flavoring grain (the same style that other brands like Pappy Van Winkle and Old Fitzgerald make). The distillery expanded into wood finishing with the launch of Maker’s 46 in 2010, but this wasn’t your typical cask-finished whiskey. Instead of putting bourbon into a new set of barrels, the distillery inserts 10 virgin French oak staves that have been seared into cask-strength Maker’s, and lets the whiskey age for a little more than two months in its cool limestone cellars.
Maker’s expanded its lineup with the Wood Finishing Series in 2019, releasing a series of bourbons given unique stave finishes over the ensuing years using different types of wood that are seared to different levels. According to master distiller Dr. Blake Layfield, searing really means using infrared to “cook” the wood, as opposed to toasting or charring it, thereby releasing specific chemical compounds which will then flavor the whiskey. The Wood Finishing Series kind of ended in 2023, but then began a new chapter in 2024, and is said will wrap up again in 2028. It’s a little confusing, but now we have the first release in the World Wood Collection, which is being released exclusively at global travel retail locations.
Expedition 01 is the first Maker’s bourbon to use mizunara, the Japanese oak that is known for being rare, expensive, and often difficult to work with due to its porous nature. It’s also highly coveted for the flavors it imbues into whiskey. Of course, it helps that Maker’s Mark is owned by Suntory Global Spirits, the Japanese company that also controls House of Suntory and happens to have access to a great deal of mizunara barrels. According to Layfield, the amount of mizunara devoted to this bourbon was actually quite small, but it still had a significant impact. The exact percentages of staves used for this release are as follows: 55 percent American oak, 40 percent French oak, and 5 percent mizunara. The bourbon was initially matured for seven years and then spent nine weeks in the distillery’s limestone cellar to finish.
I was able to try each component on its own before tasting the final blend, and indeed they all have their own unique character. Despite it being just a fraction of the overall blend, this bourbon does read as mizunara-influenced, which is a testament to the impact even a small amount of that type of wood can have on a whiskey. As you sip, there are the usual incense and floral notes that you’d expect from the use of this Japanese oak, but those are fairly subtle and balanced out by flavors like maple, vanilla, dark wood, leather, apple, and toasted almond. Unlike past Wood Finishing Series releases that were bottled at relatively high ABVs, this clocks in at 47.5 percent, or 95 proof, which I think is really much more enjoyable to drink.
Of course, as mentioned before, this is currently a global travel retail release that you can find at JFK, London, Istanbul, Perth, and Bengaluru (SRP $85). On one hand, the brand is positioning this as a special release for the duty-free market that should draw in consumers looking for something new; on the other hand, this could be seen as a testing ground. Does that mean Expedition 01 could be a wider release in the future? Perhaps, but in the meantime if you’re traveling through one of these airports, pick up a bottle. You won’t be disappointed.
Flicker is currently Robb Report's whiskey critic, writing a weekly review of the most newsworthy releases around. He is a freelance writer covering the spirits industry whose work has appeared in…

articles.title_orig: Map Shows How States Mark Columbus Day As Trump Vows To Protect Holiday
articles.title_zh: Map Shows How States Mark Columbus Day As Trump Vows To Protect Holiday
articles.content_orig:
Americans will mark Columbus Day tomorrow, Monday, October 12, but how they celebrate depends solely on where they live.
The extent of their engagement centers on whether they get a paid day off, celebrate indigenous people or other commemorations, or simply continue with a normal working day.
The different approaches among states come as Donald Trump has renewed his defense of Christopher Columbus and pledged to protect his legacy.
On Friday, Trump hosted a Columbus Day Celebration at the White House, ahead of the federal holiday.
The administration had already issued its 2026 Columbus Day proclamation on October 7, saying Americans should " honor his life of valor, adventure, and ingenuity " and "pledge to safeguard his story." The proclamation strongly stated that the administration would "never allow his legacy to be erased by radical extremists."
Earlier this year, a replica of a Columbus statue originally built by Ronald Reagan which had stood in Baltimore since 1984 was installed on the White House grounds after “rioters tore it down and threw it into Baltimore Harbor on July 4, 2020.”
Columbus Day is a federal holiday, but its observance at the state level is far from uniform.
https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30530019/
An analysis by Pew Research Center found that 30 states recognize Columbus Day in some form, while only 20 make it a paid holiday for state government employees.
Other states have either replaced it with Indigenous Peoples Day, recognize both occasions, or don’t make either a state holiday, and treat it as a normal day.
The differences reflect the longstanding debate surrounding Columbus' legacy.
Native American advocates and other critics have opposed celebrating him because of his treatment of Indigenous people and the consequences of European colonization, while Columbus Day has historically also served as a celebration of Italian American heritage.
Trump, meanwhile, has embraced Columbus as part of his broader effort to defend what his administration portrays as traditional American historical figures and symbols.
According to Pew Research Center's analysis, in almost all of the 30 states that recognize Columbus Day in some form, it falls on the second Monday of October, although Washington state fixes its Columbus Day observance on October 12 and Puerto Rico commemorates Columbus' arrival there on November 19.
The states that make Columbus Day a standalone paid holiday are:
Seven states share Columbus Day with another observance:
The other five share the day with Indigenous Peoples Day:
Another 10 states recognize Columbus Day as a public or legal holiday or another formal day of recognition, but without giving state employees a paid day off.
Tennessee takes an unusual approach. Although the state officially observes Columbus Day, its governor can, and routinely does, shift the observance to the Friday after Thanksgiving so communities get a four-day weekend, according to Pew.
Delaware dropped Columbus Day entirely in 2009, replacing it with a floating holiday that state workers can take on a day of their choosing. In 2019, Maine, Vermont and New Mexico, along with the District of Columbia, replaced their paid Columbus Day holidays with Indigenous Peoples Day.
California has also routinely used an official proclamation to recognize Indigenous Peoples Day.
Oklahoma uses another formulation. It marks the second Monday of October as Oklahoma Native American Day, which is an unpaid day of observance. The state separately observes Indian Day and has a law requiring the governor to declare a day honoring each tribe on a date chosen by that tribe.
Another 18 states don’t commemorate Native Americans on the second Monday in October but do have Native American-related observances at other points in the year.
The diverging state policies contrast sharply with the position taken by the Trump administration.
In his 2026 proclamation, Trump called Columbus a "legend" and said his "vision, fortitude, and perseverance" helped set historical events in motion that eventually culminated in the creation of the United States.
The president also directly addressed attempts to remove Columbus from public commemoration, saying: "We are forever indebted to his courageous voyage, and we will never allow his legacy to be erased by radical extremists."
That position continues the approach Trump took in 2025.
In last year's proclamation, he accused "left-wing radicals" of toppling Columbus statues, vandalizing monuments and attempting to "erase our history." He also described Columbus as a "true American hero."
In a Truth Social post, Trump also wished Americans a "Happy Columbus Day," singling out the Italian American community and again criticizing the removal of statues of Columbus. He said the "days of plunder are over," adding that the statues were "back, more magnificent than ever."
"This is a big day for our great Italian American Community, and the Country of Italy itself, maybe the biggest," Trump wrote.
The split over the second Monday in October has developed over decades.
Columbus Day was first observed as a federal holiday in 1937 and was originally associated strongly with Italian American heritage, according to Pew. In 1971, the holiday moved from October 12 to the second Monday of October.
In more recent decades, Native American organizations and other critics have pushed governments to replace Columbus Day, pointing to Columbus' treatment of Indigenous people and the consequences of European settlement.
Anthony Tamburri, dean of the John D. Calandra Italian American Institute at the City University of New York, told Newsweek that the differences between states and cities are partly connected to their Italian American populations. He said cities and states with established Italian American communities have traditions of celebrating Columbus as a figure who " brought together two worlds ," while places with smaller Italian populations may not have the same tradition. "States and cities determine whether to celebrate it or not. This is why we have the three different circumstances of (1) Columbus Day, (2) Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples’ Day, (3) Indigenous Peoples’ Day."
Historian Philip Deloria, a professor at Harvard University, also previously told Newsweek that Columbus Day's history is also intertwined with efforts to combat anti-Italian prejudice and position Italian immigrants and their descendants within a shared American identity. He said, “Columbus Day has its roots in violent anti-Italian/anti-immigrant sentiments and practices in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and its elevation as a holiday had a lot to do with efforts to combat those sentiments and to position the Italian immigrant and Italian descent communities in relation to a shared sense of Americanness.”
At the same time, he said Columbus' own writings and accounts of his voyages showed his plans for Indigenous populations included enslavement, raising the question of why Indigenous Americans would celebrate him.
Ben Railton, a professor at Fitchburg State University, previously told Newsweek : "We desperately need a holiday focused on Indigenous Americans; and it also would be great to have one focused on actual Italian Americans and that community and heritage."
Columbus Day falls on Monday, October 12, 2026, with federal observance continuing nationwide but state governments marking the date in markedly different ways.
Trump's comments and his 2026 proclamation signal that, at the federal level, his administration intends to continue explicitly championing Columbus and the Columbus Day holiday. State approaches, however, range from paid Columbus Day holidays to Indigenous Peoples Day observances, combined commemorations, and states where the second Monday in October is an ordinary working day.

articles.title_orig: SUN: Isaias sets record as latest Atlantic hurricane, drenches Maryland
articles.title_zh: SUN: Isaias sets record as latest Atlantic hurricane, drenches Maryland
articles.content_orig:
by MATT HUBBARD & KARL HILLE | THE BALTIMORE SUN
This GOES-19 GeoColor satellite image provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and taken at 1:06 p.m. EDT, Friday, Oct. 9 2026, shows Hurricane Isaias approaching the Gulf Coast of Alabama and Florida . (NOAA via AP)
MARYLAND (WBFF) — Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 Hurricane but has since been downgraded to a Post-Tropical Cyclone. Despite the reduction in strength, the storm now holds the record for the latest start to the Atlantic season, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
At least four deaths were linked to the storm, the Associated Press reported, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.
The Maryland Transit Authority warned that “Wet roads will be a concern throughout the day, with periods of heavy rain likely,” in a post on X. “If you’re heading out, slow down, leave extra space between vehicles, keep your headlights on, and watch out for standing water. Never drive through a flooded roadway. Stay safe!”
The administration said Isaias formed Wednesday, Oct. 7 and is the latest first hurricane of the Atlantic season since at least 1905, when the first Atlantic hurricane also formed on Oct. 7. The administration noted that Isaias is also the first Atlantic hurricane in nearly a year; the last being Hurricane Melissa, which formed Oct. 25, 2025 — just over two months after the 2025 season’s first hurricane, Hurricane Erin, formed.
